state.misconception_label: Believes f(x - a) translates the function up a units

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: What transformation maps the graph of \(y=f(x) \) to the graph of \( y=f(x-3) \). I got Translation by vector
\(
\left[\begin{array}{l}
0 \\
3
\end{array}\right]
\) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of it like this: Imagine you have a toy car on a track, and you move the starting point of the track to the right by 3 units. How does the car's position change? Try applying this analogy to the function \( f(x-3) \) to see if it helps clarify the transformation.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, so like... if the track moves right, then the car would be in a different position on the track? So does that mean f(x-3) moves the graph to the right by 3 instead of up? But I'm still confused about why it's the x that changes and not the y...

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of it this way: imagine you have a piece of string representing the x-axis, and you shift the starting point of the string to the right by 3 units. How does this affect the position of the points on the string? This analogy will help you understand why it's the x that changes in \( f(x-3) \) and not the y.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses analogies that don't directly address why the student confuses x-shifts with y-shifts, and while the student begins to recognize the horizontal shift in Turn 2, they remain confused about the fundamental x vs y distinction by Turn 3, showing minimal progress on the core misconception.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete, everyday analogies (toy car on a track, piece of string) to help the student understand the abstract concept of function transformations, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
